title: Short Stuff: The Great American Coin Shortage of 2020
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 2020 American coin shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. The hosts explain that although roughly $48 billion in coins was in circulation in April 2020, the coins were not moving because coin-heavy businesses (arcades, laundromats, public transit, convenience stores) closed or reduced hours, and the U.S. Mint slowed production and furloughed workers. Stores posting exact-change-only signs, offering gift cards or charity round-ups instead of change, and a push toward card payments hurt cash-dependent customers, including the unbanked and low-income Americans. A letter from retail trade groups to Fed Chair Jerome Powell and Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin complained about coin shipment rationing to banks. The Mint raised production to 1.2 billion coins a month in June and 1.35 billion for the rest of the year. Suggested fixes include spending coins, taking them to banks or Coinstar. The episode closes with the fact that a U.S. coin stays in circulation up to 30 years versus about 18 months for paper bills.

segments.title: Opening banter and coin shortage sign
segments.summary: The hosts open with a joke about a 'there's a coin shortage' line and describe signs in U.S. stores asking for exact change or card payment because they have no change. They note the U.S. Treasury counted about $48 billion in circulation in April 2020, but the coins are not moving.

segments.title: Why coins stopped circulating
segments.summary: Coin-heavy businesses like arcades, laundromats, public transit, and convenience stores closed or cut hours during the pandemic, breaking the flow of coins. The U.S. Mint slowed production and furloughed workers. Many businesses shifted to card-only payments and contactless transactions.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the coin shortage discussion.

segments.title: Stores' workarounds and the retail groups' letter
segments.summary: Some stores offered charity round-ups or gift cards instead of change, which hurt efficiency and customers who needed their change. The National Grocers Association and other retail groups wrote to Jerome Powell and Steven Mnuchin in June, complaining that coin shipments to banks were being rationed.

segments.title: Cash dependence and who is affected
segments.summary: Households with low income and unbanked Americans rely on cash because banks and credit card companies do not serve them. Cash makes up a large share of small transactions, about half of all U.S. transactions of ten dollars or less, so the shortage hurts them and small businesses.

segments.title: Mint production increase and ways to help
segments.summary: No quick fix exists, so the hosts expect circulation to return to normal over time. The Mint raised production to 1.2 billion coins a month in June and 1.35 billion for the rest of the year. Suggested actions include spending coins, taking them to banks, or using Coinstar, which the Fed promoted, and the 'get coin moving' campaign.

segments.title: Coin lifespan and sign-off
segments.summary: A U.S. coin stays in circulation up to 30 years, compared with about 18 months for paper bills. The hosts sign off.
